courses.title: 1. Understanding Mind and Body
courses.subtitle: Why performance pressure is a protective reaction – not a defect.

lessons.title: Accelerator and Brake
lessons.summary: The dual control model: why desire depends not only on stimulation, but on what is putting on the brakes.
lessons.content:
You want to feel close. Then your erection fades, lubrication doesn't come, or everything happens sooner than you hoped. Suddenly, your attention leaves the touch and settles on a question: Is something wrong with me? A moment you wanted to enjoy has quietly become a test.

Why it works
An image from sex research helps make sense of this shift: arousal has an accelerator and a brake. A familiar scent, a touch, a fantasy can draw you in. Stress, tiredness or the worry that you aren't enough can hold you back. Excitation and inhibition work alongside one another; they needn't pull in the same direction. Perhaps something that appeals to you is missing. Perhaps something is getting in the way of desire. Sometimes, both are true.
Physical responses are part of this picture too. During arousal, blood vessels in the pelvis widen, allowing more blood to flow in. Under stress the body switches to alarm, stress hormones narrow the vessels, the pelvic floor tightens, and in men ejaculation can come faster.
There needn't be any danger around you. Even the quiet thought “I hope it works tonight” can bring tension into a familiar moment.

The exercise
Make a small list with two columns. On the left: What presses your accelerator? For example a certain scent, time without hurry, a way of kissing. On the right: What presses the brake? For example an untidy bedroom, the phone, the worry of taking too long.
Stay with the right-hand column for a moment. What could change? What needs a conversation, or simply more time? You don't have to talk your body into anything. You're learning what makes closeness easier for you.

When to see a doctor
If erection or wetness stays away permanently, even without pressure and when you're alone, a medical examination is worthwhile. In men, erectile problems can be an early sign of cardiovascular disease.
lessons.reflection_question: At what moment do you typically feel your system switch from pleasure to tension – and what happened just before?

lessons.title: The Vicious Circle of Anticipatory Anxiety
lessons.summary: How a single experience leads to being in alarm mode before anything starts – and where to break the circle.
lessons.content:
Almost everyone experiences situations where the body doesn't play along – because of tiredness, alcohol, stress or simply not being in the mood. Normally you write it off as a bad day.

Why it works
It can become distressing when a single experience is interpreted as a catastrophe. The next time, you no longer go into the situation with anticipation, but with a silent test question: “Will it happen again?”
That creates a circle. First: an intimate situation begins. Second: the memory triggers tension before anything has happened. Third: you start watching your own body with suspicion. Fourth: the tension presses the brake from the first lesson. Fifth: if the feared difficulty happens again, it can seem to confirm the fear.
Cognitive behavioural therapy starts at the second step: with automatic thoughts. Sentences like “If it doesn't work tonight, I've failed” feel like facts, but they are judgements. And judgements can be checked.

The exercise
Write down the sentence that first goes through your head when closeness is about to happen. Then ask yourself: Is that really true? What would I say to a good friend who thinks this way? Phrase a more realistic sentence, for example: “My body had a bad day. That says nothing about me or our relationship.”
The reframing journal in the app takes you through exactly this exercise step by step.

When to see a doctor
If the anxiety weighs on you heavily or you avoid closeness permanently, sex therapy can be very helpful. Seeking support is not a sign of weakness. It can help you understand and change this cycle.
lessons.reflection_question: Which sentence shoots through your head first when an intimate situation is about to happen – and what would a kinder, more realistic sentence sound like?

lessons.title: Audio Practice: Releasing the Brake
lessons.summary: A guided breathing exercise with a double inhale to signal to the body: there is no danger.
lessons.content:
Make yourself comfortable for the next three minutes. You can sit or lie down. Close your eyes if you like.

We'll now use a simple breathing technique that may help you feel calmer: the double inhale with a long exhale. Experts call it the physiological sigh.

Breathe in deeply through your nose. If it feels comfortable, follow with a small second inhale without forcing your lungs to fill. Now let the air out very slowly through your slightly open mouth. For as long as it feels effortless. If you feel dizzy or short of breath, return to your normal breathing.

Very good. Twice more. Breathe in deeply through your nose. A little sip of air on top. And breathe out long, soft and completely. You may notice your shoulders settling a little.

One last time. Breathe in deeply. Top up briefly. And let everything go. Let your lower jaw relax. Release your tongue from the roof of your mouth.

Now simply let your breath flow. Bring your attention to your lower belly. As you breathe in, the abdominal wall gently rises; as you breathe out, everything softly sinks back.

Right now there is nothing to achieve, nothing to check and nothing to reach. Your body may simply become heavy. Stay here for a few more breaths.
lessons.reflection_question: How do your shoulders and jaw feel now compared with three minutes ago?

courses.title: 2. The Anatomy of Arousal
courses.subtitle: More than three zones: how the whole body feels pleasure – and how to find your own map.

lessons.title: Arousal Is a Whole-Body Event
lessons.summary: What happens in the body as pleasure grows – far beyond the genitals.
lessons.content:
When people talk about arousal, most think of three places: penis, breasts and clitoris. Yet arousal is an event of the whole body. It begins in the head, shows on the skin and runs through breath, heart and pelvis.

What happens
Arousal involves the nervous system, blood flow and perception working together. Genital erectile tissues fill with more blood, including those in the penis, clitoris and vestibular bulbs beside the vaginal opening. Lips, nipples and earlobes also receive more blood and become more sensitive. Breathing deepens, the heart beats faster, and in many people the skin on the chest and neck flushes.
Arousal can also change how touch feels. A sensation that was neutral a moment ago may become more intense.

Why it works
In surveys where people rated their body zone by zone, mouth and lips, breasts and nipples, nape, neck and inner thighs came far ahead after the genitals. Women and men differed much less than many think. And almost every part of the body was named as arousing by someone.
The order matters as well. What is too much at the start can be wonderful in the middle of arousal. That is why it pays to begin with the zones further out and to approach the centre slowly.

The exercise
Take ten minutes and observe your body as pleasure arrives, alone or together. Where does it get warm? Where does it tingle? Where does the skin become more sensitive? Remember three places outside the genitals that respond too.

Consent and safety
Every body responds differently, and the same body responds differently on different days. There is no zone that has to be arousing.
lessons.reflection_question: Which place outside your genitals responds when pleasure arrives – and did you already know?

lessons.title: Head, Ears, Neck and Nape
lessons.summary: Why slow, light touch on the head and neck sets off so much.
lessons.content:
The head is full of nerves. The lips are among the most sensitive places of the body, the scalp can be sensitive to the movement of hair, and the neck and nape have thin skin that hardly anyone touches in everyday life.

Why it works
In hairy skin, which means almost everywhere except the palms and soles, there are special nerve fibres, the C-tactile fibres. They report less where you are touched and more how it feels. They respond most strongly to slow, light stroking with a hand at skin temperature, a few centimetres per second, although the most comfortable pace varies from person to person. In studies, people describe such touch as especially pleasant, and many find it calming.
The ear has one more special feature: part of the outer ear is supplied by a small branch of the vagus nerve, a nerve involved in relaxation, among other things. Whether that explains why gentle stroking of the ear feels so cosy to many is not settled. What is certain: the ear is sensitive, and a breath there gives many people goosebumps.

The exercise
Stroke yourself or {P:your partner} from the ear over the neck to the shoulder. First at your usual pace, then half as fast, then half as fast again. Which pace feels most comfortable to you?
Also try: fingertips circling over the scalp. A gentle pull on a handful of hair, close to the roots. Lips brushing over the nape without kissing.

Consent and safety
The neck is vulnerable. Pressure on the front of the neck does not belong in an exploration, not even playfully. Some people don't like sounds or wet kisses at the ear. Ask each other.
lessons.reflection_question: Which pace felt the most beautiful – and is it slower than the one you usually touch with?

lessons.title: Back, Belly, Backs of the Knees and Feet
lessons.summary: The forgotten surfaces – and why they in particular can awaken pleasure.
lessons.content:
Back, belly, the backs of the knees and the feet are often skipped during sex. Yet they are large, calm surfaces on which arousal can build well.

Why it works
The back offers a large area of skin, much of which is difficult to reach yourself. Touch there often feels like being held, and for many, feeling held is the door to pleasure. The skin over the sacrum, the flat area above the buttocks, is supplied by nerves from the lower spinal cord, the same region as the pelvic floor and genitals. Some feel warmth and pressure there all the way into the pelvis. Whether that is because of this proximity is not proven – just try how it feels for you.
The lower belly lies over the bladder and the uterus or prostate, close to the inner parts of pleasure. The backs of the knees and the insides of the wrists have thin, soft skin. And the feet are full of nerve endings. Some people find touch there relaxing; others do not enjoy it.
A frequently heard explanation is that in the brain the feet lie right next to the genitals, which is why they are arousing. Newer measurements suggest, however, that the genitals are represented closer to the hip. So why many people find feet erotic remains open. It is enough that it feels good.

The exercise
Let yourself be touched for ten minutes only on the back, belly, backs of the knees and feet, or touch yourself there. At the end, lay one warm hand flat on the sacrum and the other on the lower belly and breathe between both hands. Notice whether something stirs in the pelvis.

Consent and safety
Feet and the backs of the knees are ticklish for many. Some prefer steadier, broader contact. If touch remains uncomfortable, leave that area out. During pregnancy, touch the belly only gently, and if unsure, ask your midwife or doctor.
lessons.reflection_question: Which of these forgotten surfaces would you like to be touched on more often?

lessons.title: Chest, Perineum and Buttocks – in Every Body
lessons.summary: Zones that every body has and that are often attributed to only one sex.
lessons.content:
Nipples are often seen as female, the perineum as an insider tip for men, the buttocks as taboo. In fact every body has these zones, and in every body they can give pleasure.

Why it works
Chest and nipples: in many people, regardless of sex, the nipples become erect when touched, and some feel it all the way into the pelvis. A small brain-imaging study in women found that touching the nipple also stimulated the brain area where touch to the genitals arrives. That is an interesting clue, but no proof that it is the same for everyone. Many men also enjoy being touched on the chest but don't dare to say so.
The perineum, the place between the genitals and the anus: the pudendal nerve, which also supplies the genitals, runs here. The deeper structures nearby depend on individual anatomy. The clitoral crura run along the pubic bones; pressure on the perineum does not provide a simple way to target them directly.
The buttocks and the anus: the skin around the anus is densely packed with nerve endings. For some, a flat, warm hand on the buttocks is already enough; others like more. Both are fine, and none of it has to happen.

The exercise
Explore the chest with different kinds of touch: a flat hand, fingertips circling around the areola, a light tug, a breath of air. Then the perineum: lay two fingers flat, press gently, release, small circles. Notice how your pelvic floor responds.

Consent and safety
Nipples are very sensitive for some people, for example before a period or while breastfeeding. At the anus, always use lubricant and short nails, and never move from the anus to the vulva or into the vagina without first washing hands or toys. More on this in course 11.
lessons.reflection_question: Which of these zones have you so far not credited your own body with?

lessons.title: Your Own Map
lessons.summary: Draw a body map of your pleasure – and swap it with your partner if you like.
lessons.content:
Textbooks offer general maps. You can gradually discover which kinds of touch you enjoy. Drawing it is one of the most beautiful ways to get to know yourself.

Why it works
Knowing your preferences makes them easier to communicate during an intimate encounter. And whoever knows their partner's map touches with more confidence and less pressure.
The map changes: with the cycle, mood, age and level of arousal. A place that is unpleasant at the start can later be the most beautiful.

The exercise
Draw two simple outlines on a sheet of paper, from the front and from the back. Then explore your body zone by zone, for example with the guided self-exploration. Afterwards, colour it in: green for “very much”, yellow for “sometimes” or “only later”, red for “rather not”. Write down what kind of touch you like in a place: light, firm, warm, slow.
If you are in a relationship: ask {P:your partner} to draw a map too. Swap them and tell each other what surprised you. Then try out a green spot on the other's map that you have never touched before.

Consent and safety
Red stays red until the person changes it themselves. A map is an invitation, not a contract, and today may be different from yesterday.
lessons.reflection_question: Which place on your map surprised you?

courses.title: 3. Every Body Is Beautiful and Sexy
courses.subtitle: Out of comparison, into feeling: how women and men can see their bodies with kind eyes and feel desirable in them.

lessons.title: The Myth of the Perfect Body
lessons.summary: Where the idea of the “right” body comes from, and how varied the bodies of women and men really are.
lessons.content:
An image stays with you: a flat belly, broad shoulders, skin without a blemish. What you see has been selected, lit and often edited. Advertising, social media, films and porn offer a narrow view of human bodies. When that view becomes your measure, it is easy to lose sight of how varied people really are. This affects women and men, even when the ideals they encounter differ.

Two ideals, one problem
Women are often shown a slim, firm, smooth body: a flat belly, firm breasts, not a trace of cellulite, no hair except on the head. Men are often shown a tall, muscular body: broad shoulders, a six-pack, full hair, a big penis. Both ideals have one thing in common: very few people look like that, and even they often only with good lighting, the right pose and photo editing.

How varied bodies really are
Skin: it has pores, moles, freckles, spots, redness, scars and stretch marks, in women and men alike. The vast majority of women have cellulite, including very slim women.
Hair: everyone grows body hair, sometimes thick, sometimes sparse, on the legs, armpits, belly, chest, back and around the genitals. Many men lose hair on their head over the years; that's very common and not a weakness.
Belly and bottom: bellies are round, soft, and have folds or rolls when you sit. Bottoms are flat or round, firm or soft.
Chest: breasts differ in size and shape, often even the two breasts of the same woman. Nipples are light or dark, large or small, flat or protruding. Men have a chest too, which can be flat, muscular or soft.
Height and build: bodies are tall or short, narrow or broad, sturdy or slight. None of these shapes is naturally more attractive than another.
Genitals: labia can be short or long, and the two sides are usually different. Penises are straight or curved. When soft they are sometimes smaller, sometimes larger, and that says little about how big they get when aroused. Testicles often hang at different heights.
These differences are part of the variety of human bodies.

Why comparison hurts so much
Our brain compares automatically. Seeing lots of edited images quietly shifts our inner yardstick. At some point your own, perfectly normal body starts to look like a mistake. It is worth questioning the yardstick you use to measure your body, too.
On top of that: anyone who struggles with how they look is often half in their head during sex. Instead of feeling, they watch themselves. That costs pleasure, which is exactly why it's worth changing this way of looking.

The task
For one week, notice which body images you come across: on your phone, in ads, in films. Each time, briefly ask yourself: is this real or staged? And what feeling does this image stir in me?
If you like, also follow a few people or projects that show real, unedited bodies, of women and of men. Many find that this changes how they see themselves, too.
lessons.reflection_question: Which image of a “right” body do you carry around with you, and where does it come from?

lessons.title: A Kind Look in the Mirror
lessons.summary: Describing instead of judging: a mirror exercise for women and men that quietens the inner critic.
lessons.content:
Looking in the mirror can become a quiet inventory: too much belly, too little muscle, another crease. Perhaps you already know the place your gaze returns to each time. Habits like these build over years. You can begin to make room beside them for another way of looking, one that starts by simply noticing.

Describing instead of judging
The first step isn't to find everything beautiful. That would be asking too much. The first step is to look neutrally. Experts call this body neutrality: seeing your body as it is, without judgement.
Instead of “my belly is too fat”, you say: “My belly is round and soft.”
Instead of “my thighs are awful”: “My thighs are strong and carry me.”
Instead of “I hardly have any muscles”: “My arms are slim.”
Instead of “my hair is getting thin”: “My hair is thinner than it used to be.”
Neutrality is a bridge between rejection and affection. Once you stop putting yourself down, there's room for kindness.

The task
Stand in front of a mirror for ten minutes, clothed or naked, whatever feels right for you. Make sure the light is pleasant and nobody will disturb you.
Let your gaze wander slowly from top to bottom: hair, face, neck, shoulders, chest, arms, hands, belly, hips, bottom, genitals, thighs, knees, calves, feet. Describe each part in one neutral sentence, out loud or silently.
When a judgement comes up, notice it without condemning yourself for it, and rephrase it neutrally.
Finally, name three things you like about your body and three things you're grateful to it for. For example: my hands can be tender. My legs carried me to work today. My skin feels every touch.

If it's hard
That's normal, especially at first. Start with five minutes. Repeat the exercise a few days in a row. With time, the inner critic may grow quieter. There is no change you have to notice after a week.
If looking in the mirror weighs on you heavily, for example if you spend hours preoccupied with one body part or withdraw because of it, talk to a doctor or a psychotherapist. There's good help for this.

Going deeper
The guided body journey below this lesson continues the exercise with your hands: feeling instead of looking.
lessons.reflection_question: Which neutral sentence about your body felt surprisingly good?

lessons.title: Sexy Is a Feeling, Not a Measurement
lessons.summary: What attraction really is about, and how women and men can feel desirable in their bodies.
lessons.content:
Sometimes what stays with you after meeting someone is a voice, a laugh or the way they move. Attraction has many sides; measurements alone tell us little about what draws us to a person. Your own sense of being at home in your body can grow, too. Clothing, music or a moment of feeling alive can offer a beginning.

What attraction is about
Many people say they fell in love with someone who wasn't their “type” at all. Attraction arises in contact: when someone feels seen, when someone is relaxed and genuine, when there's humour and warmth. Self-assurance can play a part, alongside physical preferences. And self-assurance doesn't mean finding yourself perfect, it means not constantly hiding.

What makes you feel sexy
For some it's a particular piece of clothing: lace, a well-fitting shirt, jeans you feel good in. For others music, dancing, a scent, freshly washed hair, a well-groomed beard or simply a well-rested morning. For some it's movement: sport, yoga, a walk after which you can feel your own muscles.
It isn't about how you look to others, but about how you feel in your body.

The task
Write a list of five things that make you feel sexy or alive. Choose two and do them deliberately this week, just for you. A few ideas:
Wear underwear that feels good, even if nobody sees it.
Dance in the kitchen to a song that moves you.
Take time for body care: lotion, shaving or deliberately not shaving, a warm bath.
Walk more upright for a day, with a soft belly, relaxed shoulders and an open chest.
Look at a photo of yourself where you liked how you looked, and ask yourself what you felt back then.

How posture feels
Posture and feeling are linked. Standing tall, letting your shoulders drop and breathing deep into your belly often changes how you feel inside too. Sucking in your belly and holding your breath, on the other hand, keeps you tense. Try both deliberately and notice what they do to you.

For couples
For one week, give each other a compliment about the other's body every day, and make it concrete: not “you look good”, but “I love how your shoulders look when you stretch”. Whoever receives the compliment just says “thank you”, without playing it down.
lessons.reflection_question: Which of the five things on your list makes you feel most like yourself?

lessons.title: Lights On: Letting Go of Shame in Bed
lessons.summary: When the light has to go off or the blanket has to stay on: how women and men can quieten shame together.
lessons.content:
You are close to someone, yet part of you is watching from outside: how does my belly look? Can I let go of the blanket? What can my partner see? Worries about skin, hair, muscles or genitals can come between you and the touch. This lesson invites you to bring your attention gently back to what you feel.

What really counts
Often your partner pays attention to completely different things than you do: to closeness, to desire and to you letting go. The belly you see so critically is often simply part of the person they desire. Your partner may wish you could feel at ease. That does not create another obligation to hide your insecurity.

Talking about it
Shame gets quieter when you say it out loud. In a calm moment, not in bed, tell each other which parts of your body make you feel insecure. Then the other says what they like about exactly these parts, or simply find normal. Listening is enough, without contradicting or sugar-coating.

The task for two
Take an evening with warm, dimmed light. Undress each other slowly. Whoever is undressing says one sentence with each piece of clothing about what they find beautiful or attractive about the part that's just been revealed. Whoever is being undressed says nothing except “thank you”. Then you swap.
When you're both naked, lie down next to each other and stroke each other for a few minutes with just your eyes and fingertips, without a goal.

If it's too much
Start smaller: candlelight instead of the ceiling lamp, a shirt that may stay on, or one part per evening. There's no obligation to have the light on. There's only the invitation to show a little more of yourselves, bit by bit.

For singles
The exercise also works alone in front of the mirror: undress slowly and give each part that's revealed a kind sentence. And for the next time with someone new, this thought may help: you can meet someone new without first having to feel completely confident or beautiful.
lessons.reflection_question: What surprised you most about what your partner finds beautiful about you?

lessons.title: When Your Body Changes
lessons.summary: Pregnancy, ageing, illness, scars: how women and men can stay kind to their bodies, even as they change.
lessons.content:
You have known your body for years, yet it can suddenly feel unfamiliar. A change in your skin, a scar, a different weight: the familiar picture no longer quite fits. Transitions like these can take time. They may also change how you experience closeness and desire.

What can change
For women: after pregnancy, the belly, breasts and skin often change, and stretch marks or a caesarean scar remain. During menopause, skin, weight, hair and vaginal moisture change.
For men: over the years, hair on the head often thins, the belly gets rounder, the muscles get softer. Erections take more time or more direct touch. After prostate surgery or with some medications, erection and ejaculation can change.
For everyone: weight changes, operations, accidents, chronic illnesses, breast surgery, a stoma, scars and skin changes. And simply ageing, with wrinkles, age spots and grey hair.

Grief is allowed
If you miss a body you used to have, that's allowed. Forbidding yourself this grief or brushing it off with “just be grateful” doesn't help. Acknowledging it often clears the way to making friends with the body you have today.

Your body has been through something
Some marks recall something joyful; others bring difficult experiences to mind. A scar need not tell a comforting story, and you may not feel grateful for a changed belly. You can acknowledge what your body has been through and still feel sad, angry or uncertain about it.

Getting to know closeness and desire again
Many couples discover new forms of closeness precisely after changes: more time, more touch across the whole body, less fixation on the same old routine. Those who stay curious often find paths they never had in view before.

The task
Place a hand on a part that has changed or that you struggle with. Breathe calmly into it a few times. Say silently: “Thank you for carrying me through all of this.” If it feels right, stroke it slowly with a little oil. If you're in a relationship, you can invite your partner to touch this part together with you.

Good to know
Changes can affect sexuality too, for example altered sensation after an operation, dryness during menopause or erection problems. Much of this can be treated well, for example with lubricants, local hormones, medication or pelvic floor training. Talk to a doctor if something is weighing on you. It isn't an embarrassing topic, it's everyday business in any practice.
lessons.reflection_question: What can you thank your body for today, even if you don't like everything about it?

lessons.title: Wrapped up: lingerie for every body
lessons.summary: Sexy lingerie isn't just for models: how women and men find underwear they like themselves in.
lessons.content:
Perhaps practicality has usually guided your choice of underwear. Another question can have a place beside it: how would I like to feel wearing this? A soft fabric, a colour or a cut can speak to a side of you that gets little room in daily life. Lingerie belongs to no single body ideal. It can fit the body you have today.

Why lingerie can change so much
What we wear on our skin changes how we move and how we feel. Many people say that in beautiful underwear they walk differently, sit up straighter and look at themselves more kindly in the mirror. That holds true even when nobody else sees it.

For women
There is much more than the classic push-up bra. Soft bralettes without underwire, bodysuits that flatter the whole upper body, camisoles of silk or satin, high-cut briefs that make the legs look longer, lace, mesh, stockings with suspenders. Good shops and brands offer lingerie in many sizes, including for large breasts, wide hips and round bellies. Many women with a soft belly feel especially good in high-waisted briefs or a bodysuit. Others love to show their belly.

For men
Men have more options than grey boxer shorts, too. Snug trunks, skimpy briefs, underwear made of mesh or sheer fabric, silk shorts, an open shirt over bare skin. For many men the thought of dressing up for their partner is unfamiliar. Yet many partners find exactly that very attractive: that he makes an effort and wants to show himself.

How to find what suits you
The size: underwear that pinches or cuts in doesn't feel sexy. Get advice or measure yourself. Sizes vary between brands; the number on the label is not a judgement of your body.
The fabric: silk and satin are cool and smooth, lace is playful, cotton is soft, mesh is cheeky. Touch the fabric and imagine how it will feel for a whole evening.
The colour: black and red are classics. Dark green, burgundy, midnight blue or a shade close to your skin tone can be just as beautiful.
Your favourite spot: which part of yourself do you like? Your bottom, your back, your shoulders, your chest, your legs? Look for lingerie that shows off exactly that spot.

The exercise
Pick a piece of lingerie you would never normally buy and try it on, in the shop or at home in front of the mirror. Don't pay attention to what bothers you, but to what it does to your posture. Then wear it for a whole day under your normal clothes. Nobody needs to know.

For couples
Choose lingerie together, in a shop or on the sofa. Each person picks one piece for themselves and one for the other. Anyone who doesn't want to wear something says so, and it isn't up for discussion. And don't forget the men: he gets to be wrapped up nicely, too.
lessons.reflection_question: Which piece of lingerie surprised you by how good you felt in it, and which part of you did it show off?

courses.title: 4. Escaping the Spectator Trap
courses.subtitle: How to stop checking yourself from the outside during sex – and get back to feeling.

lessons.title: The Spectator Trap
lessons.summary: Why self-observation during sex works like a director switching on the floodlights in the middle of the scene.
lessons.content:
Part of you is in the encounter. Another part is checking how you look, what your body is doing and whether everything is going well. Masters and Johnson called this inner watching spectatoring. We call it the spectator trap: attention shifts from experience to evaluation.

Why it works
When you are aroused, you are normally right in the middle of it: you feel warmth, skin, scent, movement. Worrying and planning may fade into the background.
In the spectator trap the opposite happens. Inwardly you step next to the bed and watch yourself with a clipboard: “Is my body working right now? Am I taking too long, is it too fast? How do I look? What is my partner thinking?”
The tricky part: checking whether you're aroused disturbs exactly what arousal needs – letting go in the moment. Arousal can no more be forced than falling asleep. Constant checking can make it harder to stay with what you feel. And the observing itself presses the brake from course 1.

The exercise
Get to know your inner examiner. After your next intimate encounter, or after time on your own, note down: What questions did it ask? What did it pay attention to?
Give it a name, preferably a slightly ridiculous one. Once you recognise your examiner, you can greet it kindly next time – and turn back to what there is to feel right now. The next lesson shows how.
lessons.reflection_question: What does your inner examiner focus on most when you slip into the spectator trap?

lessons.title: Feeling Instead of Checking: The Art of Attention
lessons.summary: How to steer your attention away from brooding and back into your senses – with three simple anchors.
lessons.content:
The inner examiner is talking, and you find yourself listening when you would rather stay with the touch. Trying to silence it can give it even more room. Instead of fighting the thought, you can offer your attention somewhere else to settle: a temperature, a texture, the contact of a hand.

Why it works
Attention has limited space. If you direct it fully onto one concrete sensation, less is left over for worrying thoughts. This is the core of sensate focus, the touch exercises developed by Masters and Johnson, which are used in sex therapy.
What matters: the point is not to create arousal through touch. Touching to test whether it arouses you is already the spectator trap again. You feel just to feel. Arousal may arise; quiet touch without arousal has a place here too.

The exercise
As soon as you notice you're drifting off in your head, pick three qualities of the touch that is happening right now:
First, temperature: Where is the skin warm, where is it cool?

Many people know pain during sex, especially often women and other people with a vulva, some only occasionally, some every time. Some spend a long time finding words for it, out of shame or fear of disappointing their partner. Yet pain is a signal, not a part of sex you have to endure.

Why this happens
The causes are varied: too little lubrication or arousal, infections, skin changes, scars, endometriosis, hormonal changes after giving birth or in menopause. An overactive or painfully tense pelvic floor can also play a part.
On top of that there's a circle: expecting pain makes you tense up. A tense pelvic floor makes penetration more painful. The next pain confirms the expectation. The exercise

Second: learn to release the pelvic floor. The letting-go exercise in the pelvic floor timer is made for this: breathe in, widen, yield.
Third: when penetration is added again, the person who had the pain decides everything: whether, when, how deep, how fast. Plenty of lubricant, positions in which she is on top, and stop at any time. Have pain checked by a doctor, for example a gynaecologist, especially if it's new, strong, burns, bleeds, keeps coming back or persists. lessons.title: When the Erection Doesn't Play Along

Why this happens
An erection involves nerves, blood vessels and the smooth muscle of the erectile tissues working together. Anxiety, pressure and constant self-monitoring can interfere with that response. A possible clue: if erections in the morning or when alone are as usual, that suggests tension or the situation play a big part. It doesn't rule out physical causes, though, and often both work together. If they're missing permanently, the body should be examined by a doctor.

Third: talk about it. Many partners relate a missing erection to themselves. A sentence like “It has nothing to do with you, my thoughts got in the way” relieves you both.

Why it works
